text: Agile is a set of values and principles rather
than a single prescribed process In this lesson we
examine Scrum Kanban Extreme Programming and Lean Software Development
and explain how testing changes with each approach Start
with a comparison that will remain useful throughout the
course Imagine a team building a customer portal while also
receiving production support requests Its planned feature work benefits
from a clear short-term goal but incoming incidents do
not respect a sprint calendar No single label solves
both problems The team must decide how to plan
how to visualize active work and how to build
reliable software Scrum provides a framework for product work
Kanban helps manage flow X P contributes engineering practices
Lean encourages attention to value and waste Evaluate the
problem before selecting the vocabulary
Scrum organizes complex work into sprints commonly one to
four weeks Consider a customer management portal During planning
the team selects a registration story The Product Owner
clarifies acceptance criteria including valid addresses invalid addresses and
duplicate registration Developers and testers collaborate during the sprint
and stakeholders inspect the increment at the Sprint Review
The Retrospective identifies ways to improve Testing is integrated
throughout the sprint rather than postponed to its final
days Walk through a Scrum example The Sprint Goal
is to let new customers register safely The team
selects registration and email verification because they support that
goal A tester asks whether duplicate email addresses are
allowed and what happens if a confirmation message arrives
late Developers and testers discuss these examples while work
is still small During the sprint they inspect progress
and adapt their plan If registration passes its happy
path but bypasses verification the team has not established
the intended outcome Finishing tasks is useful only when
the increment meets the agreed quality conditions and supports
the goal
Kanban visualizes work and limits work in progress A
maintenance team may use Backlog Ready Development Testing and
Done columns If Testing has a work in progress
limit of three and already contains three items the
team focuses on completing existing work rather than starting
more This makes bottlenecks visible and supports steady delivery
especially for teams receiving unpredictable support requests Now move
the same work onto a Kanban board Three registration
fixes are already in Testing and the team's illustrative
testing limit is three A developer has finished a
fourth change Simply pushing it into Testing hides the
capacity problem Instead the team investigates why existing work
has not finished Perhaps accounts cannot receive verification messages
in the test environment Helping restore that environment may
finish more valuable work than starting another feature Work-in-progress
limits are a signal to collaborate They do not
mean that an overloaded person must work faster and
they are not a substitute for understanding the system
Extreme Programming or X P emphasizes engineering practices including
test-driven development pair programming and continuous integration In T
D D a developer writes a failing test writes
enough code to pass it and then refactors safely
This Red Green Refactor cycle works well for calculations
and business rules Testing becomes part of writing the
software rather than a separate final checkpoint Consider X
P through a concrete calculation The portal grants a
ten-percent introductory discount on an eligible purchase of one
thousand rupees Write a test expecting a discount of
one hundred Run it and confirm it fails for
the expected reason Implement the smallest change that makes
it pass Then improve the code while the check
stays green Add an ineligible-customer case expecting zero discount
This creates a feedback loop in which examples guide
the design Refactoring matters repeatedly adding special cases without
improving the design can produce brittle code even when
individual tests pass
Lean focuses on customer value and reducing waste Waste
in testing might include waiting for test environments duplicate
paperwork or slow feedback from an oversized test suite
Lean does not mean skipping important tests A team
might run fast smoke tests on each commit and
more comprehensive regression tests later preserving coverage while reducing
feedback time Lean invites a different question where does
the customer wait without receiving additional value Suppose every
small change waits two days for a shared testing
environment Buying another reporting tool might not reduce that
delay The team could provide reproducible environments isolate test
data or run a smaller set of checks earlier
Before changing the process record the current delay and
its cause After the experiment compare the results Reducing
waste does not mean removing evidence needed to judge
quality It means avoiding work and waiting that do
not help deliver a useful dependable outcome
A feature-development team may benefit from Scrum a support
operation may benefit from Kanban a calculation-intensive product may
benefit from X P practices Teams can combine approaches
The right selection depends on delivery constraints technical risk
and team maturity Here is a selection exercise with
three fictional teams Team A builds a new portal
and needs frequent stakeholder feedback around a product goal
Scrum could help structure that inspection Team B maintains
several systems and receives unpredictable requests Kanban could help
expose queues and manage capacity Team C changes financial
calculations frequently X P practices such as test-driven development
and continuous integration could strengthen technical feedback These are
starting hypotheses not universal prescriptions Each team should inspect
its constraints run a small process experiment and decide
whether actual customer outcomes and feedback speed improve
Combining approaches requires clear policies A Scrum team might
visualize work with a Kanban board and limit the
number of stories actively being developed It might also
use pair programming for risky calculations and run unit
tests on every commit None of those practices removes
Scrum's accountabilities or events Problems arise when a team
adopts labels while dropping the useful feedback loops behind
them Write down how new work enters when testing
begins what Done means and how urgent incidents affect
planned work Those agreements are more actionable than saying
the team is simply hybrid
For your practice task imagine that ten support requests
arrive while a portal team is implementing a planned
registration improvement Identify the most urgent customer risk then
describe how you would make the incoming work visible
Decide which active item you would finish before starting
another Finally choose one engineering practice that could prevent
the same defect returning A strong answer connects the
delivery process to a testing action and an observable
result For example address a production access problem add
a focused regression check and review whether interruption policies
preserved visibility into the remaining feature work
A useful way to compare approaches is to follow
one change from request to feedback Take an urgent
password-reset defect First identify the customer impact and make
the work visible Decide how it enters the team's
current work under an explicit policy Next agree on
examples for a valid link an expired link and
a reused link Use small technical checks to guide
the fix then verify the integrated recovery journey Finally
inspect the delay from recognizing the problem to obtaining
reliable evidence Scrum Kanban X P and Lean contribute
different ideas to that same journey None removes the
need to clarify the rule implement safely or evaluate
the result
Now consider a misleading process improvement A team shortens
its sprint from two weeks to one week and
expects quality to improve automatically But its test environment
still takes three days to restore and stories still
arrive without examples The shorter calendar exposes the problem
more often without removing it A more useful experiment
might make one environment reproducible or split one large
story into independently verifiable slices State the expected improvement
before trying it then inspect the outcome This is
how process choices become learning rather than ceremony When
discussing a methodology in an interview or a team
meeting connect it to a constraint and a concrete
feedback loop
Scrum emphasizes iterative inspection Kanban focuses on flow X
P strengthens engineering discipline and Lean reduces waste Knowledge
check which approach would help a support team receiving
unpredictable requests and why Subscribe to Tech at sixty
